# The POPL 2019 paper against the judgement: what changes

## In short

- The paper confirms the large calls: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat, the 2009 overload sentence gone, the three rules, the return-type rule in the form batch 7b's rung C plans, applicability and specificity on declared quantified domains, and the implicit bound `Any`.
- It contradicts one default and one mechanism, both in batches not yet run or cheap to change: item 30's "least instance" is the 2012 rule the paper says the team could not prove and abandoned; the checker's binding of an unconstrained type parameter to `Bottom` (rows 447, 425, 516) is what the paper's model forbids outright. The paper's rule for both is the same sentence: instantiate at the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the call's static return type, never at the value's type alone and never at `Bottom`.
- It adds four things the record lacked: that rule; the exact form of the overloading rules with "existential reduction"; a restriction that its proof needs (a method type parameter may not appear in another's upper bound), which the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families break; and a phase-5 requirement, that the dispatcher must know the call's static return type at run time.
- Three things should be done differently, all cheap: item 30's sentence in 7b's rung S and one test pair in rung C; the `Bottom` binding replaced by the bound in one checker rung, which replaces the "treat as a throw" fix the judgement recommended for row 447; row 516's union replaced by the bound. Nothing on route A, answer 9, item 26 or the conversion order changes.

## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says

The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:

- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).

## 1. The verdicts the paper bears on

### 1.1 Route A: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flattened (D4)

- The paper confirms the rule and the flattening. [Anc-Same-Trait] is the exclusion in the paper's own terms, and "because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait" (p. 11:11, lines 550-554). There is no tower, no self type and no `comprises T` in it (searched).
- It adds one thing the route-C notes could not know: variance cannot rescue the tower. The self-typed algebra traits put their parameter in a parameter position (`opr =(self, other: T)`), and [D-Method] forbids a covariant parameter there (lines 571-572, 584-592). So `Equality[\+T\]` is ill formed, and the covariant clause of the ancestor rule, the only clause that admits two instances on one chain, is closed to the tower. The patents' forest rule stays what the record called it, a sketch outside the group's proven model.
- Nothing to do differently. One line for batch 7b's rung S: Appendix I's instantiation-exclusion entry cites [Anc-Same-Trait] beside the 2011 paper and the 2012 Types chapter.

### 1.2 Answer 9: the overload sentence goes, the three rules, the return-type rule over every instance (D17)

- The paper confirms the drop and the rules: a generic declaration "is applicable to a type α if there exists an instance D of d that is applicable to α" (§ 2.2, p. 11:5, lines 246-248); "we use the subtype relation of their domain types as in Allen et al. [2011]" (§ 4.1, line 604); the three rules as Figure 5 states them.
- It confirms rung C's planned form of the return-type rule. The record plans "the paper's special arrow, `∀[Δ1, Δ2] (S1 ∩ S2) → T2`, with the less specific declaration's parameters kept quantified except where the domain reduction forces an equality" (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md:93`); that is [Return-Test] with the paper's reduction in a narrower form.
- It adds the general form of that reduction (§ 4.2, lines 733-743, with the `ArrayList`/`List` example at lines 676-683 and 731-732): collect the constraints that keep the intersected domain off `Bottom`, solve them, and compare the reduced domain. The record's reduction forces equalities through instantiation exclusion only; the paper's also carries bounds it cannot solve as constraints. The difference is a family of valid overloads the revival's checker will refuse and the paper's accepts.
- Do differently: nothing in the decision. Rung C's decision record names the paper's reduction as the general form and its own as the special case; rung C's tests add the paper's `ArrayList`/`List` triple as a program, expected to be refused today and gated as an expected failure if it is. Cost: one paragraph and one test in a rung already in batch 7b.

### 1.3 The positional rule (answer 9's revival addition)

- The paper has no such rule. Type parameters are α-renamed ("We assume the conventional α-conversion to rename bound variables", line 669) and a dispatched declaration is instantiated by substitution from the ilks and the static return type ([Dispatch], line 874-879), never handed the call's written static arguments by position. So an override that reorders its parameters is well formed in the paper's model.
- The positional rule exists because the team's code generator passes written static arguments by position to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row 398). It guards an implementation habit, not a rule of the designers' model. It refuses nothing in the library (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7.md:234`).
- Do differently: keep the guard, since the code generator still has the habit, but batch 7b's rung S states it in a callout as a restriction of the compiled implementation pending run-time instantiation by substitution, with the paper cited, not as a rule of the language; phase 5 lifts it when the dispatcher instantiates as [Dispatch] does. Cost: wording in an entry rung S already writes.

### 1.4 The conversion-and-overloading decision of 2026-09-28 (D25, decision 1)

- The paper has no coercion, so it is silent on the order "convert only when nothing fits". It confirms the two halves the decision rests on: applicability when some instance fits (line 246-248) and specificity on declared, quantified domains (line 604, Figure 6).
- It adds a caution about what its proof covers. Its well-formedness rule (2), "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" (lines 565-570), excludes every F-bounded generic function: the library's `SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]` and `PROD` of answer 7, its `BIG MAX[\T extends StandardMax[\T\]\]`, and every function over `T extends Integral[\T\]`. The record's option-2 soundness note already found that the readings part exactly at the F-bounded shapes (`reviews/option-2-soundness.md:14`, `:54`, `:110`). So the paper's Theorem 5.11 does not cover the library's reductions, and the record should not cite it as covering them. Where such a parameter is fixed by an invariant argument type (`Generator[\T\]`), the bound is checked and never solved, which is why both the team's checker and the revival's handle it; the paper's restriction protects its one-pass solve, not those calls.
- Do differently: nothing built. The decision records of rungs S and C say in one sentence that the paper's soundness result excludes F-bounded method type parameters and closed types, and that the library's reductions rest on the 2011 rules as implemented, not on the 2019 proof.

### 1.5 Item 26: `comprises` read at the level of values, with run-time uniqueness (D27)

- The paper omits closed types and nominal exclusion and says both "can be added in an obvious way" (lines 142-144, 1302-1303). So it neither confirms nor contradicts the coverage reading, the Meet Rule's closed-trait case or row 492's repair.
- It adds one fact for the proof appendix. Theorem 4.1 (§ 4.3, p. 11:15, lines 782-789) keeps static uniqueness: No Duplicates makes the more-specific relation antisymmetric, Meet makes every applicable set a meet semilattice, and "there always exists a unique most specific method declaration". The revival's addendum gives static uniqueness up for run-time uniqueness at a call whose argument's static type sits between two closed traits (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md:8-9`, `:115-116`). In the paper's model the same case would be met by the team's own plan of 2009, identifying the intersection of two closed traits with the union of their common subtypes (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:285`), under which [Meet-Third] holds with a single meet and Theorem 4.1 stands. Item 26's judgement did not weigh the paper on this (searched: no citation).
- Do differently: no change to batch 7b; this is the one place the revival's type theory steps outside the designers' last proven model, and it should be said. Rung S's entry for the proof appendix says in one sentence that FGFV keeps static uniqueness as a theorem, that the coverage case is beyond FGFV, and that the revival gives up static uniqueness there on the addendum's premises. Cost: one sentence.

### 1.6 Item 30: a generic declaration beside a plain one at run time (D28)

- The paper contradicts the default and gives the rule. The record chose "the instance the value fixes, the least instance where it fixes none", Welterweight's rule (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:189-192`: "l_j is the type inferred for P_j", the lower bound), and recorded Naden's return-type restriction as future work, weighing Naden's 2012 objection that programmers could not follow execution without static types (`literature.md` § 1). The paper, with Steele among its authors, took the other road: static return types are carried to run time ([R-Method], lines 888-896), and the instance is the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the static return type's constraint, never the lower bound alone (lines 1274-1284). It says in so many words that the lower-bound rule could not be proven.
- Where the two rules agree: a parameter fixed by an invariant position in a parameter type (`grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])`), since lower and upper bound coincide, which is the case the judgement's example and rung W's row 157 concern. Where they differ: a parameter that is the whole type of a parameter or occurs only covariantly. `id[\T\](x: T): Box[\T\]` called through `r: Any = id(z)` with a `ZZ32` value gives `Box[\ZZ32\]` under the record's rule and `Box[\Any\]` under the paper's; a later dispatch on the box tells them apart.
- Where they meet answer 8: the revival's static promotion instantiates `op[\T extends Number\](z, w)` at `ZZ64` and annotates the call's result `ZZ64`; the paper's run-time rule then gives `Number ⊓ ZZ64 = ZZ64`, the same instance. So the paper's rule reproduces rung I's static choice at run time from the annotation, which the "least instance" rule does not promise.
- Walk cannot apply the paper's rule: it has no static types, so no static return type to constrain the instance; the value's type is all it has. That is walk's limit, as for coercion (judgement, item 7).
- Do differently, in batch 7b: rung S states the paper's rule as the designers' latest word in the dispatch paragraph (the dispatched declaration's parameters instantiated at the intersection of their upper bounds under the call's static return type, never `Bottom`), and states in a callout that both implementations today take the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter, walk by necessity and the compiled path until phase 5. Rung C adds one expected-failure pair for the case where the two rules differ (the `Box[\Any\]` shape above) beside the two it already adds. Rung W's row-157 fix stays, being walk's best. Phase 5's list gains one line: the dispatcher needs the call's static return type, which the team's code generator does not pass (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:2048`, "Not sure what to do with return type"). Cost: wording in a rung that already edits the passage, one test pair, one plan line.

### 1.7 The implicit bound `Any` (Q1; the judgement's item 3)

- The paper confirms it: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (lines 418-419). The judgement's item 3 stands with this as its deciding citation; rung S cites it in the callout that revises `trait-parameters.tex:49-50`. Nothing else changes.

### 1.8 Row 447, the written `extends Object` bound, and every `Bottom` binding (D23 decision 2; the judgement's commission error 1 and item 2)

- The paper contradicts the mechanism and gives the fix. Its type system "requires that both static and dynamic type inference algorithms instantiate type parameters with non-Bottom types" (lines 845-847, 884, 1119-1120), the solving step "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom" (lines 1005-1006), and an otherwise unconstrained parameter takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, `Any` by default, and the static return type's constraint.
- Under that rule the crashes of row 447 do not arise. `fail[\T\]("...")` in a `ZZ32` value position is instantiated at `ZZ32`; `r: Any = et(z)` instantiates `et` at `Any`, and `BoxT[\Any\]` is a class that exists, where `BoxT[\Bottom\]` carried as `java/lang/Object` was not. The compiled checker's solver does the opposite today: an inference variable left open is bound to `BOTTOM` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1954-1955`, `killIvars`; `Formula.scala:524`), which is why rung B's written bound "works" and why the kept expected type of rung I still binds `Bottom` (row 447's later notes). The Working Draft's own note asks "Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers BottomTypes for static parameters?" (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:233-234`); the paper is the designers' answer.
- This replaces the judgement's item 2. Treating a `Bottom`-typed call as a `throw` in the code generator was a repair of the symptom; the paper's rule removes the cause and is the designers' own, and it reaches row 425 (a generic big operator's no-argument form bound to `Bottom`), the interpreter's counterpart row 424 (walk erases an unwritten static argument to `Bottom`; it should take the bound), and the inference chapter's callout (`inference.tex:212-215`), which today describes the `Bottom` binding as the checker's behaviour.
- Do differently: one checker rung, in batch 8 or beside rung Q in batch N's second run, that binds an inference variable with no lower bound to the intersection of its upper bounds instead of `BOTTOM`, with row 447's two probes and row 425's `SUM[j <- lo#i] (3 j)` as its tests (row 425 may need the big-operator desugaring's bounds as well; the rung measures it); rung B's written `extends Object` lines become unnecessary and may stay; one walk rung for row 424 later. The inference chapter's callout and its Appendix I entry change in the same batch. Cost: two small rungs; it removes a phase-4 prerequisite the judgement had ranked first among the errors of commission.

The chapter gives such a parameter "the union of the types of those arguments" (`inference.tex:95-98`); the paper says that is the assumption the team could not prove, and takes the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound or `Any`. ### 1.10 The `covariant` keyword (row 404; answer 6's road back)

- The paper confirms the direction and is the specification for it: the marks, the position check, the ancestor rule under variance, dispatch with marks, and the cost. It also confirms answer 6's road back: phantom covariant parameters appear in no position, so they pass [D-Method] trivially.
- Nothing to do now; it is off the path. Row 404 and worklist item 12 point to the paper as their design when they are built.

### 1.11 Walk's run-time choice of coercions (the judgement's item 7)

- The paper is silent on coercion. But its whole dynamic semantics needs the static types of invocations at run time (lines 329-331, 820-824), which walk does not have. So walk cannot implement the designers' last model of dispatch either, and the judgement's reading, walk's run-time choice accepted as the interpreter's limit and the compiled path following the text, is strengthened. Nothing changes; the road to a walk that matches is static types under walk, his wish of 2026-09-15.

- Phase 4's natives, the sized model, decision A's store, the algebra bounds: the paper has no library, no `nat` parameters, no unboxing; silent.
- One addition to phase 5's list, from 1.6 and 1.8: the compiled dispatcher must receive the call's static return type. Without it the paper's instance rule cannot be applied at run time, and the return-type check that makes generic-beside-plain sound under variance is unavailable. The team's code generator does not pass it.
- One addition to phase 6's, from § 5.4: the paper expects run-time instantiation to cost "relatively low but nonzero" in the invariant case and names caching and dynamic recompilation for the variant ones (lines 1263-1273). MicroGPT's generics are invariant.

### 1.13 Row 508 and the attempt order (the judgement's item 4)

- Silent: no coercion in the paper. Item 4 stands as written.

## 2. Verdicts the paper leaves untouched, by name

F1, F2, F3 (its ranking of texts is confirmed, not changed), D1, D2, D3, D5, D6 (rows 329 and 330), D7, D8, D9, D10, D11, D12, D13, D14, D15, D16, D18, D19, D20 (sizes; the paper has none), D21, D22, D23's decisions 1, 4 and 5, D24, D25's decision 2, D26, D29, and the judgement's items 1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 11.

1. Batch 7b, rung S (not yet run): item 30's dispatch sentence states the paper's instance rule, with today's "value's type" behaviour in a callout (1.6); the positional rule labelled an implementation restriction (1.3); the implicit bound's callout cites the paper (1.7); row 516's union sentence replaced by the bound (1.9); one sentence each on static uniqueness in the proof-appendix entry (1.5), on the paper's exclusions in the overloading entry (1.4), and [Anc-Same-Trait] in the exclusion entry (1.1). All in files rung S already edits. Cost: wording.

Batch 8, or batch N's second run beside rung Q: one checker rung replacing the `BOTTOM` binding by the intersection of the upper bounds, tests from rows 447 and 425, the union candidate replaced by `Any` (1.8, 1.9). The 2019 paper says the team could not prove that rule and replaced it: the instance is fixed by the declared bound and by the call's static result type, never by the value alone. Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/coordinator

# The coordinating session

You talk to the curator, brief the workers and keep the record. This file is the core: read it at every boot. Load a part under `references/` when you switch into its work.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**worker**
: Agent that you launch for one task: an Agent-tool subagent, a Workflow agent or a headless `claude -p` session.

**record**
: Project's memory, kept in the repository: the files that "The record: what goes where" lists.

**entry**
: Line of `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` under its permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`.

**batch**
: Run of the batch workflow script, `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, that changes the tree in several rungs and lands them together. A rung is one task of it, with its own worker and worktree.

**go**
: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work.

**ask**
: Message that puts one decision to the curator.

**boot**
: Reading that rebuilds your knowledge of the project, at session start and after each compaction.

**boot note**
: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.

**held list**
: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.

## The standing goal

You work for the curator as executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and as analyst, who finds out what happened and why.

Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide. Spend machine tokens on thinking, so that the curator's attention goes to decisions. This goal came from a compaction that left the curator "out of control, unaware of crucial details".

- Take POSITIONS, "History he knows (do not re-explain)", and the decisions in POSITIONS as known. Refer to them, and add only what is new.
- Keep your context for the curator and the record. Give exploration, tracing, surveys, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
- Start work that does not depend on a running job at once.

## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals and decides the design and process questions that you put to them. The curator does not review each commit, but carries the responsibility for the revival.

A decision is consequential if it reverses, bends or reads anew a decision on record; changes a line of the model program; touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation; chooses among ways that the record does not settle; or cannot be undone. It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing. List it in PLAN under the batch, with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A stop that holds the work.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

List every other decision for later review, a rung's small items in the gap ledger. It holds nothing up.

- Take a bare "go" as approval to start background work only.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go (`references/batch.md` has the standing go).
- Do only the work that a standing go names. Ask for any other work, even of the same kind.
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (`references/record.md`). If it settles the question, act on it. A decision asked again is the failure that the curator minds most.
- A decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- Go through re-approval rows with the curator in detail, grouped by theme.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark, but record no decision from it. Write a go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, take a deeper pass: find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. Do not halt, roll back or bisect, and invent no new fork for the curator.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix.
- When a file grows, a rule makes clutter, or a report comes that nobody asked for, propose the fix before the curator sees it.

## The facts of this environment

- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
- The curator's client can show stale state. The tree is the truth.
- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
- The context is compacted when it grows long. The boot rebuilds it from the record.
- The container can be lost, and a VM restart can take the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part). In manual mode every Workflow agent's command waits for the curator.
- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
- The platform stops the session's process about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. A stop of the turn kills every running agent.
- The git-check hook asks for a commit after every turn. Its reminders are advisory.
- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan. So a cost counts tokens written only.
- The tiers: the workers run on Opus. Sonnet does archaeology and writes nothing that the curator reads. Fable judges design questions across two areas, and runs the reviews approved in advance. Other Fable work needs a go (`references/delegating.md`).
- The curator sets this session's tier, for its register and for Fable's weekly pool. The boot note names it.

## Talking to the curator

The curator listens to most replies, so attention is the scarcest thing that you spend.

- Write plain short sentences, with contractions. Keep replies brief.
- Give advice as instructions. Use a literal phrase, not a metaphor.
- Use no flourish and no closing line that sums up. End a sentence where its point ends, with no coda after a semicolon.
- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it.
- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few numbers, each with its meaning.
- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Give the time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
- Give estimates in the project's units (a rung, a worker session), never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client.
- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.

**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:

1. The question, in one line.
2. The context, in short bullets, with a refresher first where the subject is new.
3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs.
4. What a yes commits the curator to, and what a no costs.
5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.

Give each decision a default that the curator can take without the argument, which goes in a committed review. Offer no option that does nothing.

**Quiet times.**

- When you record what the curator said, reply "noted".
- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree.
- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
- Send a push notification only for a long run's end or a stop that waits on the curator. It reaches the phone only outside the app.

**While the curator reads turn by turn.** By default you answer each point at length as it comes, and the curator falls behind in a wall of text. So hold the points:

- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of the curator's message.
- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing.
- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.

**Pages.**

- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
- The curator reads a page while iOS Speak reads it aloud at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
- Put a section's evidence and references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that listening never runs through citations.
- Give every page the house style, the CSS of the plan's page.
- Keep each live page's URL in the boot note. After a compaction, publish by that URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page.
- If a page's source is lost, rebuild it from the published page.

## The record: what goes where

Under `explorations/coordinator/`:

- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, and the parked items. Its first section says where the work stands.
- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, what to do when it ends, a question waiting on the curator, the session's tier, the next stop of the process, and the URLs of live pages.
- The held list, and the smaller items that the curator owns.
- `review-queue.md`: the items that wait for the curator's word.

Elsewhere: the reports and notes under `explorations/`, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`; and the skills. This skill holds how you and the curator work and how you run workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers, and how they read and edit the record. `cloud-container` holds the platform.

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.

- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
- Have the writer put what the curator says about how we work into its skill, as a rule (`references/skill-rewrite.md`). Until then, keep it on the held list.
- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, read these in order:

1. `CLAUDE.md`, then this file.
2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`, and give each note it reports its line.
3. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
4. The boot note, then the held list.
5. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
6. If the boot note says that a batch runs: in its batch record, the sections for the curator; the run's `journal.jsonl`; and its agents' last transcript times. Say nothing about the batch before that.

- Read nothing else. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
- Answer what is in flight from the tree, never from the curator's client.
- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
- After each start of the process, make the git-check hook a no-op again (`cloud-container`, its hooks part), and tell the curator in one line. If the permission check refuses, say that it needs manual mode.

- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch, resume or relaunch any worker.

delegating.md
# Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming workers

You brief the workers and watch what you launch. This part holds the tiers, what a brief holds, the watch on a long run, and the Workflow tool's mechanics.

**Workflow run**
: Run of a script by the Workflow tool, which launches one agent for each `agent()` call.

**journal**
: Workflow run's log, `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`. It holds one `launched` line, then a `started` line for each agent call (`key`, `agentId`, `label`, `phase`) and a `result` line with the agent's structured result.

**headless session**
: `claude -p` session started from your shell.

## Which tier runs what

- Give each worker `model: 'opus'`, the alias. An agent with no `model` takes the session's tier. Write no identifier that the alias resolves to.
- Use Sonnet for archaeology and retrieval only. It makes no judgement, and never writes a page or a text that the curator reads.
- Have an Opus worker write a longer report or page for the curator, not this session while it runs on Fable.
- Take a decision that touches two of the specification, the interpreter and the compiler in two steps. Cheaper workers gather cited evidence into a short brief. The top tier judges.
- Run a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, if all of these hold:
  - The design question touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.
  - An Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file.
  - The record does not settle the question.
- Put that judgement to the curator as an ask.
- Ask first for any other Fable worker: a question on your own conduct or a new kind of process choice, a recommendation that would reverse the curator's decision, or Fable and Opus working apart.
- Two kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: a judge's second ruling in a batch, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
- Weigh a Fable review's ideas critically, and never take them as given. Fable reviews tend to keep everything as it was. For a check, an Opus worker is enough.

A Fable token counts against the all-models limits too, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit. So Fable is not free when that pool runs low. Two workers on the wrong tier once cost 1.7M.

## What a brief holds

- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, a worker that has not read our notes lists every way that the language and the library offer.
- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
- A pointer to the research and documents on file, not a restatement of them.
- The record's measurements, as findings to cite with their sources, not claims to check again. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement of a finding only if the tree has changed under it, and say what changed.
- For a clean worker on a design fork: none of our options, but all of our measurements. It reads its question first, and measures only where no record answers it.
- The entries that it needs, quoted word for word under their numbers (`facts-extract.sh`). Quote a rule of the curator's with its measure and its example. Never restate it.
- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed, in the space that the document gives it.
- No second reader that would reframe a document.
- No request to measure, project or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
- For a page: the house style (the core, "Pages").
- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 270 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.

A worker whose task touches the repository loads `fortress-repo` by itself, and that skill tells it which choices are its own.

## Watching a run

- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, give it an estimate of tokens written.
- Watch its spend against the estimate: `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py <since-epoch> <transcript-or-dir>`.
- If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or stop it.
- Watch no other run this way. One probe once wrote 7.0M against an estimate of 0.5M.
- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: a series of `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, armed in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
- If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`). The skill writer runs so (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).

## Interrupts and stops

An interrupt, the stop of a turn, kills every running Workflow agent and Agent-tool worker. A stop of the session's process does too (`fortress-repo`, its session part). A compaction between turns leaves a Workflow run alive.

- After an accidental stop, tell the curator, and resume the run.
- Resume a Workflow run, never relaunch it: `resumeFromRunId`, with the same script and arguments as at launch, byte for byte. A finished agent keeps its result. An unfinished one runs again from its start, on its worktree's leftovers.
- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of `agent()` calls, in call order. A base given as a short hash where the launch gave the full hash misses from the first call.
- If the script has changed since launch, resume from a copy as launched (`git show <base>:<path>`). If the call order would differ, wrap `agent()` in the copy, so that the finished calls come in the journal's order of `started` lines.
- If a commit stage was killed before it committed, its edits are in the main tree. Resume with a commit prompt that names them.
- If a gather was killed mid-work, stash its staged state and move it aside before you resume.
- A new session cannot resume another session's run.
- An Agent-tool worker that a process stop killed goes on from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. One that an interrupt killed cannot be resumed. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask, and tell the new worker its predecessor's leftovers.
- Give a Fable successor the leftovers in the tree, never the transcript. The safety filter once ended a Fable worker that printed a transcript.

## The Workflow tool

- Two agents run at once on this machine. An agent costs about 45K tokens before it starts work.
- Across agents, the cache serves the first message only when the whole prompt is identical. A project agent type's system prompt is cached for every agent of the type, so put text that every agent needs there.
- A project agent type written during the session is found only after the process restarts. A project skill appears at once.
- `agent()` can return null for an agent that the harness marks failed after it delivered its result. Its work may be on its branch. The batch script's `callAgent` retries a role up to twice.
- Check a script by parsing it as an async function body, not with `node --check`. `explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js` does this.
- `explorations/coordinator/tools/journal-text.py` writes one field of an agent's result from the journal to a file.

## A second session

A second coordinating session contributes reviews and their commits, on a branch of its own from `main`. It runs no batch and changes no agreed route.

- The automatic permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go in chat: for example, a move of an earlier run's outputs back over a later run's. What to do then is in the `fortress-repo` skill's session part.

## Resuming a Workflow run

After an interrupt or a stop of the process, first read what is on disk, as the `fortress-repo` skill's session part says. A stop of the process also keeps the session ID and each Workflow run's journal.

- Resume a Workflow run. Do not relaunch it. Give the same script and the same arguments, byte for byte, with `resumeFromRunId`, the Workflow tool's argument that names the run to resume.
- At a resume, every agent that had finished keeps its result. An unfinished agent runs again from its start and finds its tree's leftovers. A relaunch would start every agent again.
- A run can be resumed only in the session that launched it: `resumeFromRunId` does not work from a new session. A run that a later resume was meant to extend cannot be finished from a new session. So write a pipeline whole into one script.

### Matching the launched run exactly

- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's `agent()` calls, in call order. It misses from the first changed call: that call and the calls after it run live.
- A base given as a short hash, where the launch gave the full hash, misses from the first call.
- If cached calls resolve at once, a script that starts calls as others finish can issue them in another order than the live run did. The resume then misses from that call.
- If the script changed since the launch, resume from a copy of the script as launched: `git show <commit>:<path>`. The Workflow harness also keeps each launched script as `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/workflows/scripts/<name>-<run>.js`.
- If the call order would differ, use a copy that wraps `agent()`, so that the copy issues the finished calls in the journal's order of their `started` lines. Do not change the prompts.
- A copy that changes only what follows the cached prefix runs the changed call live, and nothing before it. A changed prompt is a new key, so that call runs live.
- An agent killed mid-work leaves its edits in its tree, uncommitted, and any staged state. Before the resume, either name them in that agent's prompt, so that the live call checks and keeps them, or stash them and move them aside, so that the call starts clean.

### The journal

The journal is `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/journal.jsonl`. It holds one `launched` line, a `started` line for each agent call (`key`, `agentId`, `label`, `phase`), and a `result` line with the same key for each agent that returned. A resume appends to it. If a call runs live again under a key that the journal holds, the call gets a second `started` line. `explorations/coordinator/tools/journal-text.py` reads the journal. The agents' transcripts are the `agent-*.jsonl` files beside it.

- Tell the new worker what its predecessor left in the tree. Do not give it the predecessor's transcript: the safety filter has ended a worker that was told to print a predecessor's transcript.

content.content:
# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops

**prompt cache**
: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.

**interrupt**
: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.

**stop of the process**
: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.

**automatic permission check**
: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.

## The Bash tool and waits

The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).

- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s.
- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.

## Long commands

If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:

    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.

The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.

Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 270 s, such as 300000 ms. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.

    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
        done
        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
    }

## Stopping processes

Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.

Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.

## After an interrupt or a stop of the process

If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:

1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.

## When the automatic permission check refuses a call

content.content:
- **The record folded.** The FACTS entry under its area. Ledger notes through `ledger.py note`. New rows through `ledger.py add FILE --section TITLE`, each `NEW-<rung>-<n>` placeholder replaced with its number everywhere the rung's files and tests cite it, before the rung's commit. The handover line. The rung's "Revival change" section is folded into no file: both its parts are copied, word for word, into the batch's `RECORD.md` (below), and nothing is written under `.claude/`. Through batch 13 the gather folded each entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md` as the rung wrote it, and the cold reader that followed made a question's handle findable instead of deleting it: that is how the coordinator's agenda reached the skill (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there").
- **Corrections still owed.** The skeptic's `leftForGather` items. Each sentence of the specification a rung lists as made false and did not edit, corrected to what the code does, each clause checked against its code line. Batch 8's gather saw rung Q's Appendix I Effect false and let it stand, and in batch 9 no stage saw the one rung K made false. Each took a review judge and a repair, 0.53M and 0.39M (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 5; `reviews/batch-9-review.md`, section 6).
- **Text mismatches.** A text mismatch the decisions do not settle is filed, not blocking ("Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect", item 4).
- **Items for the curator.** The gather puts every item a rung, skeptic or judge returned into `PLAN.md`, under "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed" when work waits on it, else under "Off the path, parked".
- **After the rungs.** One commit closes each row a landed rung fixed (`ledger.py close N --commit HASH --test NAME`, then `ledger.py check`). One commit writes the batch's `RECORD.md`, once, last: the order and why, each rung's commit, the rows opened and closed, each skeptic's fixes and the contested rulings by commit, the rungs that did not land, the points to report, where each item for the curator went, and last, under "Revival changes, for the skill writer", each landed rung's "Revival change" section, both parts word for word.

A rung that did not land has its `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` taken out of its branch path by path, its findings folded under "Not landed", and its new rows added. None of its source is applied.

Files are staged by an explicit list and `git diff --cached --stat` is read before each commit. A commit touching a path outside `explorations/` and `.claude/` carries a `historical:` line.

## Review beside the gate

The review and the gate start together on the gather's commits. The review reads and never builds; the gate builds and never reads the record; the gate commits nothing, so the two never commit at once. Run side by side they took 14.7 minutes per batch off the serial tail. The review stays, once (P-113, "A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."). Its six checks:

1. Overlaps between rungs, and what their changes do together.
2. Each skeptic's fix and each repair commit, as applied: it does what its finding says, its test seen failing on the worker's head and then passing in its maker's transcript, a settled fix's citation, a reverted fix gone.
3. The folded record: FACTS lines, `ledger.py check`, no `NEW-` placeholder left where a row is cited, every closed row fixed, the handover, the revival-change material in `RECORD.md` true of the landed code.
4. Each specification sentence a rung listed as made false, corrected.
5. The points to report, with `holdsPush`.
6. The items for the curator, in `PLAN.md`.

What it does with a finding:

- A record-only or mechanical defect it fixes itself, inside `explorations/`, in one commit.
- A finding settled by tests and records only it routes to the next batch, as `review-routed.N` in `PLAN.md`, with no judge.
- A finding whose repair touches source, library, checker, interpreter or specification goes to a judge, who rules `land`, `repair`, `drop` or `stop`. `land` is for a ruling settled by tests and records after all: its steps go to the next batch and no repair runs.

The review returns its heads before and after its corrections and every path outside `explorations/` they changed. A path the gate reads makes the gate beside it stale, and the gate runs again. Any other path is recorded beside the gate's summary.

A review that returns nothing after three attempts holds nothing: the batch lands on its gate, and `review-missing.1` is listed.

### A review that still blocks after its repair

There is one judge and one repair for the review, and no second review. When the review's repair returns nothing, stops or does not land, the code findings the judge upheld are listed as `review-unrepaired.N` for the next batch. They do not hold the push (P-113, "A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."). A step that cannot be undone that the repair reports holds it, as a rung's does.

### A repair of tests and records only

After a repair on the merged tree, the review's or the gate's, the whole gate runs again only when the repair, or the review's corrections, changed a path the gate reads that is not a test file: under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or `build.xml` (P-114, "A tests-only repair does not rerun the gate."). In batch 8 the gate ran a second time after a repair of one sentence of Appendix I, 24 minutes on the critical path, with tables identical but for timing (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 4).

A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory.

What forces the model's 29 lines, by reading the diff (my reading):

   - 2 are the local helpers `h` and `u`, sized and taking witnesses.

   - 5 write a size that no argument carries: `corpus.tokens[\R\]`, the nine `view[\V,E\]`, the two `onehot(…, N[\V\])` lines, and the mask moved into the step, whose size `T` is the step's parameter.
   - 7 write the size of a generic function passed to the row lift, `rows(rmsn[\E\], x)`. Both paths refuse a generic function as a value without it (row 156). The specification says such arguments are inferred from context (`var-ref.tex:35-40`), and its inference chapter does not yet describe that context (`inference.tex:201-205`). With that inference built, these 7 lines would stay as they are today (my reading).
2. **D2, the vocabulary over the unsized `Array`, the model unchanged.** The products the model uses (`DOT`, juxtaposition, `rows`, `gather`, `diag`) declared over `Array[\RR64,I\]` beside the library's sized ones. No model line changes. The checker then never sees a shape, and the sized products are not what the model runs: this is the sidestep his ruling of 2026-09-19 refuses ("I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue", POSITIONS line 38).
3. **D3, the specification's own spelling of the same types.** D1 with `RR64^s` for `Vector[\RR64,s\]` and `RR64^(r × c)` for `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]` (`overview.tex:1078`, `aggregate.tex:152-170`). The same lines change; they read shorter. Measured on a six-line program (`reviews/array-design-ways/probes/pow/TPow.fss`): the compiled checker against the one library stops the component, "Desugaring MatrixType at TPow.fss:7.19 to TraitType is not yet supported" (`TPow.check.txt`); walk parses the signature and fails at the call, "Cannot unify __DefaultVector[\RR64,3\] ... with MatrixType" (`TPow.walk.txt`). Neither path takes the spelling today; it needs the type `T^n` desugared to `Vector[\T,n\]` on both.
4. **D4, sizes static from the top** (my reading, not measured). Every size of the step is a literal somewhere up the call chain if the batch size is a static choice: the check program calls the step at batch 1 and batch 4. The step then takes its sizes as static parameters from its callers, and the `reflect` bridges go; the model's api `MicroGptFlat.fsi` and the check program's calls change instead.
